claims.text: StrongDM's Software Factory is a non-interactive agent system in which natural-language seeds and end-to-end scenario harnesses drive agents that write, validate, and iterate on code under standing rules that humans neither write nor review code.

StrongDM's charter states two rules: 'Code must not be written by humans' and 'Code must not be reviewed by humans'; code is treated as opaque weights whose correctness is inferred from behavior, not inspection.

A Software Factory run starts from a natural-language seed (a few sentences, a screenshot, or an existing codebase); agents write code and run the end-to-end scenario harness, and a sample of the output feeds back into the inputs so the system self-corrects.
The Software Factory loop runs until the holdout scenarios pass and stay passing, and the code ships without human review.

StrongDM scenarios are end-to-end user-story validations, often stored outside the codebase like a training holdout set, and flexibly checked by an LLM to resist reward hacking and lazy test rewriting.
Early StrongDM experiments showed that tests alone invite shortcutting by agents, so the team shifted to externally defined scenarios representing end-to-end user stories.
StrongDM defines 'satisfaction' as a probabilistic success measure replacing boolean test-green: the fraction of all observed scenario trajectories that likely satisfy the user.
Scenario holdouts are a design claim that scenarios stored outside the codebase are less vulnerable to reward hacking; this is not proven prevention of it.

The Digital Twin Universe consists of behavioral clones of third-party services that replicate APIs, edge cases, and observable behaviors, so thousands of scenarios can run per hour without rate limits, abuse detection, or live-API cost.
The Digital Twin Universe clones Okta, Jira, Slack, Google Docs, Google Drive, and Google Sheets.
The Digital Twin Universe clones are built as self-contained Go binaries, and they can simulate dangerous failure modes that would be impossible to test against live services.
Building full SaaS replicas was always theoretically possible but economically unfeasible; agentic development reverses that cost equation.

The Factory became viable after Claude 3.5's October 2024 revision enabled 'compounding correctness' in long-horizon agentic workflows, whereas earlier models accumulated errors until the product 'collapsed'.
The initial foundation of the Factory was Cursor YOLO mode, and the validation loop uses an LLM-as-judge to evaluate satisfaction.

StrongDM's operating heuristic is that if a team has not spent at least $1,000 on tokens today per human engineer, the factory has room for improvement; this is a spend heuristic, not a measured productivity result.

StrongDM's team is three engineers who started in July 2025; by October 2025, when Simon Willison visited, they already had working demos of the agent harness, Digital Twin Universe, and satisfaction testing framework.
The captures of StrongDM's published material report principles, techniques, and model configuration but no measured outcomes of the factory's software.
What happens when a Software Factory run fails to converge is not documented.

As of June 2026, the Factory routes tasks across multiple model providers, including gpt-5.5 for everyday/DevOps tasks, QA orchestration and security review, and a consensus of opus-4.8 and gpt-5.5 for sprint planning.

StrongDM open-sourced Attractor, a non-interactive coding agent structured as a graph of phases, as a natural-language spec rather than an implementation (Apache-2.0, ~1.3K GitHub stars as of September 23, 2026), and also open-sourced CXDB, a context store for agents.
Delinea announced its acquisition of StrongDM on January 15, 2026 and completed it on March 5, 2026; whether the factory methodology continues under new ownership is unverifiable.

The factory essay reached the Hacker News front page in February 2026 (304 points, 459 comments); validation ideas (DTU, holdouts) drew admiration while the 'no human review' charter for a security product drew the harshest criticism.

Reported cautions: building the DTU required significant engineering effort, fit beyond integration-heavy domains is unclear, teams must accept not reading generated code, and the approach is less battle-tested than human-reviewed workflows.

A critic argues that applying 'no human review' to security-critical access-management software is risky, citing studies claiming AI code has 1.5-2x more security vulnerabilities than human-written code, and that scenarios are only as comprehensive as whoever writes them.

Stanford Law School commentary notes the architecture makes tracing accountability difficult, because no human reviewed the code, wrote the validating test, or built the replica it was tested against.
